library.title: Your Regulation Loop
library.shortSummary: Map trigger → automatic response → cost, then choose one better move.
library.longDescription: When stress rises, most people don’t consciously choose their behavior — they default to it. This insight helps you map your personal loop in a CBT-lite way: trigger → automatic response → cost → alternative response → recovery move. The point isn’t to judge your reaction; it’s to notice it early enough to interrupt it. Over time, this builds competence: you become someone who can handle pressure without escalation or collapse. It also supports relatedness: you can stay connected in conflict without outsourcing regulation to the other person. Use this when you notice repeating arguments, avoidance, procrastination, or emotional spikes.
questions: What is the most common trigger that flips me into automatic mode?
What is my default response (fight, flee, freeze, please, control, explain)?
What is the real cost of that response — for me and for others?
library.experiment: Next time you notice the trigger, pause for 10 seconds and choose one alternative response (one sentence, one boundary, or one break). Then do one recovery move (2 minutes).

library.title: Needs Check: Autonomy, Competence, Relatedness
library.shortSummary: Stress often spikes when one core need has been underfed for too long.
library.longDescription: Self-Determination Theory says we function best when three needs are supported: autonomy (choice and agency), competence (effective progress), and relatedness (safe connection). When one need is chronically depleted, we often compensate — overworking to feel competent, people-pleasing to feel connected, or resisting everything to regain autonomy. This insight helps you identify which need is asking for attention today. It’s not about blaming others; it’s about naming the lever you can actually move. That alone often lowers tension and increases clarity.
questions: Which need feels most deprived right now: autonomy, competence, or relatedness?
How am I compensating — and what is the hidden cost?
What is one small action that supports this need without harming the other two?
library.experiment: Choose one micro-action that feeds the missing need today (10–20 minutes). Keep it small enough to repeat.
